title: Thinking About Conceptual Understanding
author: Jemma Sherwood
summary: Responding to a post by US teacher Barry Garelick, Jemma Sherwood challenges the common conflation of 'understanding why a procedure works' with 'conceptual understanding' in mathematics teaching. She argues concepts are abstract ideas, like addition, that can never be fully explained but are progressively understood through exposure to many concrete examples across different mathematical contexts. Understanding why a specific procedure works is, she argues, a contributor to both procedural and conceptual understanding but is not equivalent to conceptual understanding itself. Her practical implication for teachers: build conceptual understanding not by demanding explicit 'why' explanations for every procedure, but by teaching the many instances of a concept in coherently related ways so pupils gradually see the underlying structure.
points: Sherwood's central distinction: understanding why a procedure works is not the same as conceptual understanding -- the 'why' is a contributing factor to both procedural and conceptual understanding but doesn't define either.

She defines a mathematical concept as an abstract idea best understood through accumulating concrete examples over time -- 'conceptual understanding is a bit like an infinite sum – we can get closer and closer but will never really get there.'

She demonstrates the idea using addition, showing how a sequence of examples across natural numbers, decimals, fractions, and surds that share the same structure deepens understanding of the underlying counting-unit concept.
Her practical takeaway: teachers can't directly 'teach' conceptual understanding, but can build it indirectly by teaching every instance of a concept in a coherent, related way.
quotes: You see, understanding why a procedure works is not the same as conceptual understanding, and as long as teachers think this, their thinking about subject will be limited.
A concept is an abstract idea, something that is, by definition, not concrete. In English literature, for instance a concept might be ‘theme’.
As we are exposed to more and more concrete examples of addition, we gain a deeper understanding of the concept of addition and its various principles, or underlying structure.
The why of a procedure is a part of both procedural and conceptual understanding and is not, in itself, the latter.
We can’t ‘teach’ conceptual understanding in the way that we ‘teach’ procedural. In the classroom, the main way we get at concepts is through procedures and their careful, coherent teaching.
